questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly outside the scope of TR90?

options.A: Contamination control management of pyrogens such as endotoxin in sterile drug manufacturing
options.B: Control of chemical contaminants, including cross-contamination between products
options.C: Control of microbial contamination in low-bioburden drug substance manufacturing
options.D: Control of foreign particulate matter in contamination-susceptible non-sterile drug products

questions.explanation: TR90 focuses on microorganisms and other extraneous materials, pyrogens (such as endotoxin), and foreign particulate matter, covering sterile drug products, low-bioburden drug substances, and contamination-susceptible non-sterile drug products. Secondary and tertiary packaging, chemical contaminants (including product cross-contamination), and intrinsic particulates are expressly excluded from the scope.

questions.question: According to the TR90 glossary, what is the definition of a contamination control strategy (CCS)?

options.A: A testing and release plan that performs sterility tests and microbiological tests before the release of each batch to confirm the final product conforms
options.B: A compilation of written procedures setting out environmental monitoring sampling locations, frequencies, alert/action limits, and the investigation process
options.C: A facility standard that classifies cleanrooms by particle concentration and sets requirements for air cleanliness and pressure differential control at each grade
options.D: A plan, based on product and process understanding, to identify, assess, control, and monitor the risks of microorganisms, pyrogens/endotoxin, and foreign particulate matter

questions.explanation: A CCS is a planned set of processes and measures to identify, assess, control, and monitor the risk of contamination by microorganisms, pyrogens/endotoxin, and foreign particulate matter, based on an understanding of the product and process, to ensure process performance and product quality. It is not a single testing plan, an EM procedure, or a cleanroom classification standard.

questions.question: Why does TR90 advocate creating a CCS document (an umbrella document)?

options.A: To bring together contamination control practices and their rationale that are scattered across procedures and reports, so they can be evaluated as a whole
options.B: To replace the details of SOPs and validation reports, so that floor personnel need consult only a single document to work
options.C: To serve as the basis for explanations to regulators so that individual batches can be exempted from final product microbial testing
options.D: To leave each contamination control measure to be managed independently by each department, to reduce interdependence and overall complexity

questions.explanation: Every pharmaceutical company already has a CCS; the practices are simply scattered across many procedures and technical documents. The CCS document summarizes these practices and their rationale and references the supporting procedures and reports so that they can be evaluated as a whole; TR90 also states that it does not replace those detailed documents but serves as a road map.

questions.question: Comparing the glossary's Alert Level and Action Limit, which statement is correct?

options.A: Exceeding an alert level requires a product impact assessment; exceeding an action limit only needs to be recorded and trended, with no investigation
options.B: An alert level indicates the process has gone outside normal operating conditions; an action limit is an early warning that has not yet departed from the validated state
options.C: Exceeding an action limit requires a written investigation, product impact assessment, and corrective action; an alert level is an early warning and also calls for investigation
options.D: For both, only the supervisor needs to be notified; written investigation and corrective action are needed only after three consecutive excursions

questions.explanation: Exceeding an action limit means the process is outside normal operating conditions, and requires a written investigation, a product impact assessment, and corrective action. An alert level is an early warning of a departure from the normal and validated state, and also calls for appropriate documented investigation (such as trend analysis), with corrective action possible depending on the outcome. The statements that reverse or confuse the two roles are wrong, and "only notify the supervisor, investigate after three consecutive excursions" is inconsistent with the investigation requirements of the glossary.

questions.question: The barrier system of an aseptic filling line has rigid walls with integral gloves; its interior surfaces are decontaminated with a sporicidal agent, it is not fully sealed, and its doors are opened only rarely under predefined conditions. Under the TR90 glossary, what type is it?

options.A: RABS (restricted access barrier system)
options.B: Closed isolator
options.C: Open isolator
options.D: Grade A air supply

questions.explanation: The glossary defines a RABS as an enclosed but not fully sealed environment with rigid walls and integral gloves, whose interior surfaces are decontaminated with a sporicidal agent and whose doors are rarely opened. A closed isolator remains sealed during operation and transfers materials through aseptic connections; an open isolator allows continuous material ingress and egress through means such as continuous overpressure; and Grade A air supply is only filtered air with no barrier requirement.

questions.question: What are the three "foundational elements" that TR90 says influence all the other elements of a CCS?

options.A: Environmental monitoring, sterility testing, and cleanroom classification
options.B: Process validation, equipment qualification, and cleaning validation
options.C: Scientific knowledge, quality risk management, and personnel awareness and quality culture
options.D: Supplier audits, change control, and corrective and preventive action (CAPA)

questions.explanation: The foundational elements in Figure 3.0-1 (dark blue) are scientific knowledge, QRM, and personnel awareness/quality culture, echoing the enablers of ICH Q10. The others are mostly individual control elements or feedback mechanisms of the quality system, not foundations.

questions.question: According to the QRM foundational element, how should the control elements of a CCS be arranged in its design?

options.A: Designed as individual control elements with redundancy, so that failure of a single element does not lead to contamination
options.B: Built around the single strongest control element, with the rest as supplements, to lower overall cost
options.C: Procedural controls used first to cover design gaps, because procedures are cheaper than engineering design and cost less over the long term
options.D: Each element validated independently, with no need to consider whether the elements work together

questions.explanation: TR90 requires the CCS to have redundancy so that a single failure does not cause contamination. If a risk is not managed in the process or facility design, procedural controls must make up for it, which actually raises cost and complexity over the whole product lifecycle; and elements that do not work together can also cause the CCS to fail.

questions.question: A process step is designed as a manual, open operation directly exposed to the environment. According to TR90, how should the surrounding CCS elements be handled?

options.A: Maintain the existing environmental controls and spot check the step once a quarter, with no adjustment of other elements
options.B: Increase the number of final product sterility test samples as compensation, leaving environmental controls unchanged
options.C: Replace strengthened environmental and personnel controls with stricter final testing, and reduce in-process sampling
options.D: The surrounding elements must be more robust, such as localized unidirectional flow, flow control, cleaning and disinfection, EM, and in-process testing

questions.explanation: An open manual step requires all surrounding CCS elements to be stronger than for a closed process, including additional technical and procedural measures. The logic of TR90 is to prevent contamination through multiple controls, not to remedy it afterward through final testing.

questions.question: How does TR90 distinguish training from education when discussing personnel awareness?

options.A: Training explains why something is done; education explains what is done and how
options.B: Training explains what the job is and how to do it; education explains why it is done
options.C: The two mean the same thing, differing only in that training is one-time and education is annual
options.D: Training is directed at management; education is directed at floor operators

questions.explanation: The document points out that training addresses "what the task is and how to do it," while education addresses "why it is done." TR90 also stresses that one-time or annual training is not sufficient to maintain continuing awareness, and ongoing reinforcement is needed.

questions.question: Which of the following is a hallmark of a sound quality culture listed in TR90?

options.A: After a contamination event, first identifying the individual at fault and imposing heavier discipline as a warning
options.B: One concentrated training a year, enough to keep all employees aware of contamination control
options.C: Treating contamination control as the sole responsibility of the quality assurance department, with floor personnel simply following the SOP
options.D: A non-blaming culture, with employees feeling ownership of product and process quality (including contamination prevention)

questions.explanation: The hallmarks listed in TR90 include a non-blaming culture, employees feeling responsible for quality (including contamination prevention), and proactive disclosure of quality risks. It also states explicitly that one-time or annual training cannot ensure continuing awareness, and that floor personnel are regarded as the real guardians of contamination control.

questions.question: What are the three main considerations TR90 proposes for assessing microbial contamination risk?

options.A: Ingress, proliferation, persistence
options.B: Ingress, detection, removal
options.C: Proliferation, identification, reporting
options.D: Source, severity, monitoring

questions.explanation: The document frames the risk assessment around three questions: how the contamination source gets in (ingress), whether environmental or process conditions allow contamination to increase or spread (proliferation), and whether cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, and monitoring are adequate to eliminate or control the bioburden (persistence).

questions.question: According to Table 4.2-1, what capability should be demonstrated when validating a sterilizing filter used for a drug product (DP)?

options.A: A 10^6 retention of viruses under worst-case conditions
options.B: A 10^3 CFU/cm² retention of molds under routine conditions
options.C: A 10^7 CFU/cm² retention of bacteria under worst-case conditions
options.D: A 10^5 CFU/cm² retention of bacteria under routine conditions

questions.explanation: Table 4.2-1 states that, where applicable, bacterial retention of a sterilizing filter should be verified at 10^7 CFU/cm² under worst-case conditions (see PDA TR26). In the same table, terminal sterilization and sterilization of equipment contacting sterile product call for demonstrating an SAL of 10^-6.

questions.question: According to Table 4.4.1-1, in a DP process, what is the current expected bioburden action value for DP bulk before sterile filtration (unless there is a scientific rationale for another volume)?

options.A: ≤1 CFU/100 mL
options.B: ≤10 CFU/100 mL
options.D: ≤10 CFU/10 mL

questions.explanation: The current expectations in the table for biologics are: ≤10 CFU/10 mL for mammalian process bioreactors and ≤100 CFU/10 mL for downstream processing; DP bulk before sterile filtration is ≤10 CFU/100 mL, with other volumes possible if scientifically justified. The value "≤10 CFU/10 mL" is the bioreactor expectation.

questions.question: Which statement about filtration and control of viruses and mycoplasma in cell culture is correct?

options.A: A 0.2 µm filter effectively removes viruses, so no further virus clearance step is needed
options.B: Mycoplasma is easily detected by turbidity or ordinary microscopy, so no special detection methods or culture are needed
options.C: The sources of viruses and mycoplasma differ greatly, so control measures aimed at viruses are of no help against mycoplasma
options.D: Viruses are not retained by 0.1 or 0.2 µm filters, while 0.1 µm filters can reduce mycoplasma

questions.explanation: Viruses cannot be removed by 0.1 or 0.2 µm filtration; they require a combination of measures such as suitable raw material sources, heat treatment or irradiation of media, adventitious agent testing, and virus clearance in the process. Mycoplasma mostly shares sources with viruses, so virus prevention measures also help; it is resistant to commonly used antibiotics and cannot be detected by turbidity or standard microscopy, and 0.1 µm filters have become the norm for media filtration.

questions.question: In-process bioburden monitoring of a process repeatedly shows sporadic contamination results. How should this be viewed according to TR90?

options.A: As sporadic, since in-process bioburden is later removed by filtration, so no further follow-up is needed
options.B: Relax the action limit so the number of deviations returns to a manageable level, and defer the investigation
options.C: It should be investigated, as it may indicate biofilm on product contact surfaces or widespread environmental contamination in the process area
options.D: Only increase the number of final product sterility test samples, with no need to investigate the condition of the process itself

questions.explanation: TR90 states that recurring sporadic contamination should be investigated because it may suggest biofilm on product contact surfaces of equipment or widespread environmental contamination in the process area. Table 4.2-2 also stresses that even where microorganisms can be removed by filtration, in-process bioburden can still cause impurities and degradation.

questions.question: An existing facility cannot achieve unidirectional personnel flow. According to TR90, what is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Nothing needs to be done, because unidirectional flow is not essential for contamination control and the status quo can be kept
options.B: Increase the frequency of environmental monitoring in place of flow controls, with no design adjustment
options.C: Rely only on stronger final product sterility testing to confirm that personnel did not cause contamination
options.D: Add procedural and design controls to prevent personnel in different gowning grades from mixing

questions.explanation: People are the main source of microorganisms in cleanrooms, so flow is critical for contamination control. Where unidirectional flow is not possible, additional procedural and design controls are needed to prevent people in different gowning grades from mixing; EM and final testing are detection means and cannot replace preventive measures in the flow.

questions.question: What three approaches does TR90 identify as most common for controlling contamination when materials enter classified areas?

options.A: UV irradiation, spray humidification, and vacuum drying before direct entry into the classified area
options.B: Chemical disinfection, successive removal of outer wrapping layers, and direct transfer through a sterilization system or an RTP
options.C: Overnight rest in a buffer zone, ventilation to remove odors, and visual inspection of appearance only
options.D: Manual wiping by personnel, central staging in a warehouse, and opening of boxes in the gowning room

questions.explanation: The three most common approaches in the text are: chemical disinfection (which must be validated, including physical wiping with a validated minimum contact time), stripping multiple layers of sterile wrapping, and direct transfer through a sterilization system (such as a double-door autoclave or e-beam) or an aseptic design connection (such as a rapid transfer port).

questions.question: Why does TR90 list "moisture" as a critical parameter of compressed gases?

options.A: Moisture makes the gas pressure unstable and thereby affects the results of filter integrity tests
options.B: Moisture makes endotoxin in the gas disappear quickly, causing endotoxin test results to read low
options.C: Moisture allows microorganisms to proliferate, and molds in particular require less moisture than bacteria and yeasts
options.D: Moisture affects only the proliferation of bacteria and yeasts, while molds are not affected by gas moisture at all

questions.explanation: The document explains that moisture is a critical parameter because it allows microorganisms to proliferate, especially molds, which need less moisture than bacteria and yeasts. Gas systems should therefore have routine monitoring, set according to QRM principles, that includes physical and microbiological parameters.

questions.question: Someone argues that "if microbial test results on a utility system pass, microbial contamination will not occur." Under the holistic approach of Table 5.1.4-1, how should this be answered?

options.A: Microbial testing has limitations; physical parameters can give early warning, and atypical trends must be responded to promptly
options.B: The view is correct: passing microbial tests is sufficient to show the system is in control, and physical parameters need no additional monitoring
options.C: Physical parameters are used only for equipment maintenance and are unrelated to contamination control; microbial results are the only basis
options.D: Only results that reach the action limit need investigation and CAPA, and other data need not be tracked

questions.explanation: The table's holistic approach points out that microbial testing has known limitations, that physical parameters can give early warning of a serious contamination risk, and that any atypical result or trend (including below the alert level) can be an early signal worth investigating.

questions.question: According to TR90's description of HVAC, how should areas with frequent personnel traffic be designed compared with less-used areas?

options.A: Maintain the same air change rate as less-used areas, adjusting only the cleaning frequency
options.B: They need a higher air change rate, because factors such as personnel traffic must also be considered
options.C: Lower the air change rate to reduce airflow disturbance of personnel movement
options.D: Raise the relative humidity to compensate for the particles generated by personnel

questions.explanation: The document gives examples: an area with heavy personnel traffic needs more air changes than a lightly used area, while an area with frequent steam operations may need active temperature and humidity control and a robust exhaust system. HVAC design must be considered together with personnel and material flows, cleaning and disinfection, and the specific risks of each area.

questions.question: Why is it inadvisable for a drug manufacturer to adopt a raw material supplier's specifications wholesale?

options.A: Supplier specifications are usually looser than the pharmacopoeia, and pharmacopoeial standards should always be used without regard to risk assessment
options.B: Specifications reflect the supplier's grasp of the material, and the drug manufacturer is not its largest user, so specifications should be set according to risk and process
options.C: Supplier specifications are approved by the regulator and therefore usually have no reference value, so they should be written entirely in-house
options.D: Supplier specifications cover only physical properties and never include any items related to microorganisms or endotoxin

questions.explanation: Specifications are often set by the raw material manufacturer according to the degree of control it knows about, and pharmaceutical use is not its largest market, so they may not be suitable. The drug manufacturer should set the relevant specifications based on the source of the material, its manufacturing process, and the quality the process requires, with the pharmacopoeia as a benchmark.

questions.question: Which statement about bioburden considerations for excipients used in sterile products is correct?

options.A: Terminally sterilized products must consider both bioburden level and identification of spore formers; sterile filtered products consider only bioburden level
options.B: Sterile filtered products must consider both bioburden level and identification of spore formers; terminally sterilized products consider only bioburden level
options.C: For both sterilization methods, only endotoxin need be tested, with no testing of bioburden
options.D: For both sterilization methods, spore formers must be identified, and bioburden level need not be considered in either

questions.explanation: The document points out that terminally sterilized products must consider both the bioburden level and the identification of spore formers, whereas sterile filtered products consider only the bioburden level. Excipients used in sterile products should be tested for bioburden and bacterial endotoxin, with the lower endotoxin limit set at least according to the calculation in USP <85>.

questions.question: When sampling sterile raw materials and excipients, what does TR90 require?

options.A: Open and sample in a Grade D environment, because the sample will still go through sterile filtration afterward
options.B: Sampling one container from each lot is enough to represent the quality of the whole lot of material
options.C: Sampling may be done in an area of a lower grade than the production environment, as long as the sampling tools are sterilized
options.D: Use closed sampling; where not feasible, sample under the same grade of environment, otherwise that unit must not be used in production

questions.explanation: TR90 requires closed sampling for sterile materials; where that is impossible, sampling must be done under the same environmental classification as production, otherwise the sampled unit must not be used in production. In addition, because microbial distribution is not uniform, sampling from every incoming container (such as every drum) is good practice and more representative.

questions.question: Which statement about control of starting materials for biologics (such as master and working cell banks) is consistent with TR90?

options.A: It is an early stage of the process, so it can be handled in a general environment, with control levels and requirements raised on entering purification
options.B: Only sterility need be tested; mycoplasma and viruses are the responsibility of downstream processing and need no separate testing
options.C: Treat as sterile material, handle aseptically in a controlled environment (such as Grade A), and test for sterility, viruses, and so on
options.D: If a cell bank is already cryopreserved, animal-derived materials need not have source documentation and records for TSE/BSE

questions.explanation: Master and working cell banks are sterile or axenic and should always be handled as sterile material, in a dedicated, controlled, closed environment (such as Grade A); they must be tested for sterility (or purity), mycoplasma, bacterial endotoxin, and viruses, and if animal-derived materials are used, source documentation for TSE/BSE control is needed.

questions.question: When human donor cells and tissues are used for ATMPs, when do GMP controls begin to apply?

options.A: Procurement and initial testing follow GCP and GCLP; GMP applies once the material is used for the ATMP
options.B: GMP applies in full from the moment of procurement, because donor cells are starting material from the outset
options.C: GMP never applies to donor cells, as long as there is full traceability
options.D: As long as there is traceability, no health assessment or risk assessment of the donor is needed

questions.explanation: TR90 explains that procurement and initial testing of human donor cells and tissues follow GCP and GCLP, not GMP; traceability and donor health assessment are the key contamination controls at the point of procurement. Once the material is manipulated or selected for use in an ATMP, it becomes a starting material and GMP applies in stages.

questions.question: According to TR90, what is the main purpose of an environmental monitoring (EM) program?

options.A: To directly prevent and control contamination in the environment so that it does not enter the process area
options.B: To replace the cleaning and disinfection program as the main documented proof that the environment is in control
options.C: To measure the performance of environmental contamination control measures and highlight possible loss of control
options.D: To prove that no microorganisms at all are present in the environment during each operation

questions.explanation: TR90 states explicitly that EM does not prevent or control contamination; through snapshots at discrete points in time, it indicates how well environmental quality is performing and reflects losses of control caused by personnel behavior, disinfection practices, HVAC failures, or facility aging.

questions.question: A site's EM trends have always been good, and a department proposes reducing disinfection frequency and dropping the sporicidal agent. How should this be answered according to TR90?

options.A: It is acceptable, because good trends prove the current disinfection practice exceeds actual need and can be scaled back
options.B: It is acceptable, but the number of EM sampling points must be increased at the same time to offset the added risk of less disinfection
options.C: Frequency may be reduced, but the sporicidal agent may not be dropped, and the department may decide the rest
options.D: It should not be done; good EM trends should not be used to support poor aseptic or disinfection practices

questions.explanation: TR90 states explicitly that an EM program with acceptable trends should not be used to support poor aseptic or disinfection practices, for example to justify reducing disinfection frequency or eliminating a sporicidal agent. EM is only a detective control and cannot replace preventive measures.

questions.question: What frequency for cleanroom requalification does TR90 section 7.1.1 mention as recommended by the current Annex 1?

options.A: Every 6 months for Grades A and B, every 12 months for Grades C and D
options.B: Every 12 months for Grades A and B, every 24 months for Grades C and D
options.C: Every 3 months for Grade A, every 6 months for Grades B to D
options.D: Every 12 months for all grades

questions.explanation: TR90 gives as an example that the current Annex 1 recommends requalification every 6 months for Grades A and B and every 12 months for Grades C and D. Periodic requalification may also be based on risk assessment, site validation procedures, or changes in trend data, or as required by local regulations.

questions.question: Comparing the two airflow patterns, which statement is correct?

options.A: Turbulent flow is used in Grade A environments to sweep away particles, and unidirectional flow is used in other classified areas to dilute particles
options.B: Turbulent flow is used in most non-Grade A areas to dilute particles; unidirectional flow is used in Grade A, where the product contacts only first air
options.C: Both have the same purpose, to dilute particles, differing only in air velocity and air change rate, with no other difference
options.D: Unidirectional flow is used only in Grade D areas to carry particles to personnel exits and out, and is not used in Grade A

questions.explanation: Turbulent flow dilutes particles and microorganisms in a cleanroom and carries them away with fresh clean air, with the air change rate set by risk assessment in the EMPQ; unidirectional flow is used in higher grade (Grade A) areas to sweep particles away from critical operations, ensuring the product is contacted only by uncontaminated first air.

questions.question: Which of the following is an "unplanned" environment or utility disruption, as TR90 gives examples, that must be addressed immediately?

options.A: Annual shutdown work
options.B: A building construction project
options.C: Preventive maintenance work
options.D: A utility power outage

questions.explanation: Planned disruptions are deliberately scheduled events such as construction projects, annual shutdowns, preventive maintenance, and equipment installation; unplanned disruptions are sudden events such as a leak in a critical utility, a power outage, or equipment repair, which must be addressed immediately. The degree of control and recovery should be commensurate with the risk.

questions.question: TR90 requires microbiology training to explain clearly the difference between cleaning and disinfection. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The purpose of cleaning is to remove physical and chemical residues; the purpose of disinfection is to kill microorganisms
options.B: The purpose of cleaning is to kill microorganisms; the purpose of disinfection is to remove physical and chemical residues
options.C: The purposes are the same, differing only in the concentration of the agent used
options.D: Cleaning targets cleanroom surfaces; disinfection targets only product contact surfaces inside equipment

questions.explanation: Training should explain clearly that cleaning removes physical and chemical residues and disinfection kills microorganisms, and should introduce the various cleaning and disinfecting agents and their uses. A regularly scheduled and validated cleaning and disinfection process is a key element of the microbial CCS.

questions.question: According to TR90, personnel who have not successfully completed gowning qualification are prohibited from entering which classified areas?

options.A: Grade A only
options.B: Grades A and B
options.C: Grades A, B, and C
options.D: All cleanrooms, including Grade D

questions.explanation: The document states that personnel are prohibited from entering Grade A and Grade B cleanrooms until they have successfully completed gowning qualification. Qualification requires multiple gowning observations and sampling of multiple locations on the outside of the garments after gowning, with sampling locations determined by risk assessment of the specific operation.

questions.question: What timing does TR90 recommend for gowning requalification?

options.A: Every quarter, regardless of whether the person has been absent
options.B: Only when gowning sampling fails
options.C: Routinely every year, or on return from a long absence
options.D: Every two years, with no requalification for those returning from absence

questions.explanation: TR90 recommends that gowning requalification be performed routinely every year, or when personnel return from extended leave or a long absence, to show that they remain competent in gowning. Disqualified personnel must take corrective action and successfully complete qualification before re-entering the cleanroom.

questions.question: According to TR90's requirements for cleanroom behavior, what is the minimum requirement for glove management?

options.A: A single layer of gloves in all areas, changed once per shift, with no additional integrity checks
options.B: Fresh sterile double gloves on every entry to any cleanroom, regardless of area grade and use
options.C: Sterile double gloves in support areas, a single layer in aseptic areas, and a change every shift
options.D: At least a single layer in support areas; sterile double gloves in conventional aseptic areas; new gloves on every entry to Grade A

questions.explanation: The document specifies: at least a single layer of gloves in support areas; sterile double gloves in all conventional aseptic processing areas; a new pair of sterile gloves on every entry to a Grade A cleanroom; and glove integrity checked at donning and before interventions, with damaged gloves replaced according to a risk-based procedure.

questions.question: A media fill in which an operator participated produced a positive (failed) unit, and the root cause was determined to be improper aseptic behavior. How should this be handled according to TR90?

options.A: Keep the operator qualified, because a media fill evaluates the process, not the individual
options.B: Only a signed undertaking is needed, with reassessment at the next annual gowning requalification
options.C: Treat as disqualified, requiring retraining and requalification, reassignment, or removal from the cleanroom
options.D: Suspend for one shift only, after which the operator may return to the original duties

questions.explanation: TR90 explains that when a media fill in which an operator participated produces a positive unit and the root cause is improper aseptic behavior, the operator is considered disqualified; after disqualification, retraining and requalification, reassignment, or permanent removal from the cleanroom is required, and there should be a procedure for disqualification and revocation of access.

questions.question: Which of the following is consistent with the considerations TR90 raises at the equipment design stage?

options.A: Use open designs wherever possible so operators can intervene and adjust at any time
options.B: Design mechanical and electrical adjustments to be made inside the aseptic area, so they can be handled immediately
options.C: Design everything level for ease of installation, with drainage handled by procedure
options.D: Use closed systems wherever possible, and design mechanical and electrical adjustments to be made outside the aseptic area

questions.explanation: Equipment design considerations include: closed wherever possible, smooth and easily cleaned surfaces, minimal human intervention in the critical zone, sterilization as a complete assembly to reduce connections, mechanical and electrical adjustments made outside the aseptic area, and design with drainage slope.

questions.question: TR90 notes that cleaning validation has limited value for predicting microbial control over the service life of equipment. What is the reason?

options.A: Cleaning validation is performed only on old equipment, and new equipment needs no such validation or assessment
options.B: Cleaning validation assesses only microorganisms and not product residues, the two are unrelated, and need not be run in parallel
options.C: Cleaning validation is performed by the supplier, so the drug manufacturer cannot know its test conditions and results, and it has no reference value
options.D: The time and number of validation tests are limited, microbial detection has limited sensitivity, and the focus has traditionally been on product residues

questions.explanation: The document explains that cleaning validation is limited by the timing and number of validation tests and by the limitations of traditional microbial testing; historically it has also focused on removing product residues, with less attention to preventing biofilm. In addition, validation is usually performed on new equipment that has not yet experienced the various wear factors.

questions.question: For single-use systems (SUS), what main risk and response focus does TR90 identify?

options.A: SUS cannot be gamma sterilized and must be autoclaved by the user before use
options.B: Leak testing is often impossible before and after use, so check the sterilization cycle, observe for leaks, and inspect welds
options.C: The tube welders for SUS need no special maintenance and can be used directly as supplied by the vendor
options.D: SUS are closed when shipped, so sterilization records and packaging need not be checked again on receipt

questions.explanation: The document notes that SUS can be sterilized by irradiation and provide a closed system; the risk is that leak/integrity testing is often not possible before and after use, so the sterilization cycle should be verified on receipt, leaks or holes observed before and during use, and tube welders correctly used and maintained (replacing blades, chips, and so on), with welds inspected before use.

questions.question: When a temporary grey space enclosure (TGSE) is used during maintenance, how should its pressure be maintained?

options.A: Lower than the surrounding classified area
options.B: Higher than the surrounding classified area
options.C: Exactly equal to the surrounding classified area
options.D: The same as the pressure outdoors

questions.explanation: TGSE planning should include differential pressure monitoring to ensure the enclosure is at a lower pressure than the surrounding classified area so that contamination does not spill out; flow, gowning and degowning instructions should also be planned, cleaning and disinfection and surrounding EM reinforced, and the post-completion recovery process defined in advance.

questions.question: What does TR90 require regarding the glove testing strategy for isolators and RABS?

options.A: Only a visual check of glove appearance each shift, with no physical testing
options.B: A glove testing strategy combining visual and physical leak testing should be defined
options.C: Only a pressure decay test once a year, with no checks otherwise
options.D: Testing only when an operator reports a glove breach

questions.explanation: Barrier technology separates operators from the process, and glove positions should avoid operators reaching over sterile product or components. TR90 requires a glove testing strategy combining visual and physical leak testing for isolators and RABS, and for RABS the time, frequency, and duration of door openings must be limited.

questions.question: According to TR90, what role does the primary container closure (primary CC) of a finished product play?

options.A: It is mainly for protecting the secondary packaging during transport and has no direct contact with the product
options.B: It is in direct contact with the drug and is the main physical barrier between the product and the external environment
options.C: It only provides labeling and lot information and has nothing to do with the microbial barrier function
options.D: It acts as a barrier only for terminally sterilized products, and is not needed for aseptically filled products

questions.explanation: The primary CC is in direct contact with the finished product and is the main physical barrier between the product and the external environment; secondary packaging protects the primary CC from microbial or foreign contamination caused by physical damage during handling and transport. CCI is critical to preventing contamination of the product throughout its shelf life.

questions.question: When does TR90 recommend starting to select and evaluate a robust container closure integrity (CCI) test method?

options.A: During product development, in parallel with the design of the CC system
options.B: After commercial manufacturing begins, depending on actual market complaints
options.C: After the process validation batches are complete, with CCI evaluation added then
options.D: At the start of post-marketing stability studies

questions.explanation: Design and development of the CC system should begin during product development; early development ensures safety in the clinical trial phase and reduces specification failures at the first formal stability studies. In addition to chemical compatibility, the functional integrity of the barrier against microbial ingress should be considered, and a robust CCI test selected during development.

questions.question: For blow-fill-seal (BFS) finished products or products that undergo vacuum in the process (such as lyophilization), what does TR90 recommend for CCI leak testing?

options.A: Probabilistic methods with sampling per batch are sufficient, with no need to test the whole batch
options.B: Test once during equipment validation, with no routine testing afterward
options.C: Check only appearance, with no leak test equipment needed
options.D: Consider deterministic leak test methods, with 100% leak testing of the entire batch

questions.explanation: Table 10.2.3-1 states that for BFS finished products or products requiring vacuum, deterministic leak test methods should be considered, with 100% of the batch evaluated for leaks; CCI for BFS should also be part of machine or mold validation, and leak tester parameters should be challenged across the range of container sizes.

questions.question: To show that the vial crimping process does not compromise container closure integrity, how does TR90 recommend verifying it?

options.A: Verify once with only the most commonly used crimping force parameters, and accept if it passes
options.B: Use only the lowest crimping force, because insufficient force is the only possible cause of leaks
options.C: Demonstrate CCI using the process parameters that produce the highest and lowest crimping forces
options.D: Check only the appearance after crimping, with no need to evaluate CCI or seal condition

questions.explanation: Excessive crimping force may crack the vial, and insufficient force gives a poor seal. CCI should therefore be demonstrated using the process parameters that produce the highest and lowest crimping forces, reflecting the worst cases.

questions.question: According to TR90, which type of container closure system requires 100% integrity testing?

options.A: Glass vials, because glass tends to have invisible cracks
options.B: Prefilled syringes, because the plunger may shift
options.C: Vial products with rubber stoppers and crimp caps, because the sealing force may be insufficient
options.D: Container closure systems that are fused on the filling line

questions.explanation: In the section on CC monitoring and testing, TR90 states that CC systems fused on the filling line require 100% integrity testing. For other containers, where design, supplier, incoming, preparation, and handling controls are robust and there is a good history, the extent of finished product testing can be reasonably reduced based on risk.

questions.question: According to Table 11.1-1, which of the following is a "predictive" metric?

options.A: Facility nonconformances such as environmental monitoring excursions
options.B: Product nonconformances such as sterility test failures
options.C: KPIs related to quality culture
options.D: Process nonconformances such as DS or raw material pyrogen/endotoxin excursions

questions.explanation: Predictive metrics include, for example, quality culture KPIs, capital reinvestment in contamination control, QRM risk reduction, and CAPA effectiveness and on-time completion; reactive metrics are the various nonconformances, such as EM excursions, endotoxin excursions, and sterility test failures.

questions.question: According to TR90, what attitude should investigations related to the CCS take?

options.A: Whenever an event is seen as a single isolated incident, assume operator error and close it
options.B: Limit the scope of the investigation to the process step where the deviation occurred, with no need to consider other elements
options.C: Decide the conclusion in advance and then support it with data to close faster
options.D: Proceed holistically, without presupposing the outcome, even if the event appears to be a single isolated occurrence

questions.explanation: Investigation is one of the feedback mechanisms of the CCS, used to find the source of contamination or to detect failure of the CCS as a whole; it should be done holistically and without prejudging the outcome, even for an event believed to be isolated. Where possible, the investigation strategy should be standardized and written into a documented plan (such as for EM investigations) to speed up handling.

questions.question: To judge whether the control strategy around a process is adequate and to identify in-process sampling locations that can monitor the effectiveness of design and controls, which tool does TR90 recommend?

options.A: HACCP
options.B: Design FMEA
options.C: A single universal risk tool that covers all risk questions at once
options.D: A simplified risk tool used only in change control

questions.explanation: TR90 gives examples: a design FMEA of the process is used to identify the best process design to prevent contamination and other failures; HACCP is used to judge whether the surrounding control strategy is adequate and to identify in-process sampling locations to monitor the effectiveness of design and controls. The document also stresses that no single tool fits all risk questions.

questions.question: What does TR90 recommend when deciding on a CAPA?

options.A: Consider only the directly affected elements, leaving other elements to be evaluated and revised at the next annual review
options.B: Consider the whole CCS, including indirectly affected elements; most CAPAs should have built-in effectiveness checks that are tracked
options.C: Have the originating department evaluate CAPA effectiveness itself, with no need to track it as any quality metric
options.D: Once a CAPA is closed, new knowledge need not be brought back into the CCS, to avoid frequent document changes

questions.explanation: TR90 requires consideration of the whole CCS (including directly and indirectly affected elements), with effectiveness checks built into most CAPAs and tracked as quality metrics; the most effective CAPAs strengthen multiple controls, and new knowledge should be brought back into the CCS during periodic lifecycle review.

questions.question: After a supplier has been qualified and approved, what does TR90 recommend for the frequency of supplier audits?

options.A: Set the audit frequency according to the criticality of the material or service supplied
options.B: Always audit once a year, regardless of the importance of the material supplied
options.C: No audits are needed after approval; manage only through the quality agreement
options.D: Audit only when a deviation or complaint occurs

questions.explanation: After a supplier is approved, audit frequency should be commensurate with the criticality of the material or service supplied; audits are a monitoring means in the contamination control framework and should cover the elements of the supplier's CCS that are fundamental to that material or service. A quality agreement should also be signed before purchase, and the supplier's CCS practices included in the qualification assessment.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the TR90 requirements for CCS governance personnel or bodies?

options.A: Authority to respond to potential adverse trends or events, and a clear escalation path to senior site management
options.B: Quality assurance expertise only, with no microbiology or process expertise, to preserve independence and objectivity
options.C: Reporting only to the head of the quality department, with no escalation to senior site management, to simplify administration
options.D: Involvement only after a major deviation occurs, with no need to periodically evaluate the state of contamination control

questions.explanation: Governance personnel must have microbiology and process expertise to understand the meaning of the data, clear responsibility for periodically assessing contamination control of the process, product, personnel, and facility/utilities and driving improvement, authority to respond both proactively and reactively to adverse trends, and an escalation path to the highest level of site management.

questions.question: According to TR90, when does the lifecycle of the CCS begin?

options.A: After the first commercial batch is produced, written up and gradually revised based on actual batch data
options.B: At the facility and process design stage, considered and documented during quality-by-design activities, as a prerequisite for GMP manufacturing
options.C: After process validation is complete, established and approved by quality assurance on the basis of the validation results and reports
options.D: Only before the first regulatory inspection, when formal documents and complete records need to be available

questions.explanation: The CCS lifecycle begins with facility and process design, should be considered during quality-by-design activities, and is formally documented as a prerequisite for GMP manufacturing; the quality system described in Section 11 then drives continuous improvement of the CCS over the product lifecycle.

questions.question: What does TR90 recommend regarding the frequency and performers of the periodic effectiveness review of the CCS?

options.A: Every three years, completed by the quality assurance department alone
options.B: Every quarter, assessed by the manufacturing department itself
options.C: Preferably annually, performed by a multidisciplinary team
options.D: Only after a major contamination event, performed by an external consultant

questions.explanation: The CCS should be reviewed for effectiveness periodically, preferably annually and by a multidisciplinary team, with the assessment covering quality trends, contamination events, change control, and validation activities, to monitor the effectiveness of contamination control for the process, product, personnel, and facility/utilities.

questions.question: What practical approach does TR90 suggest to reduce the administrative burden of the periodic review?

options.A: Shorten the review to a single year-end sign-off, omitting routine data tracking
options.B: Outsource the review to a consulting firm that issues the report alone
options.C: Review only items with deviations, with no assessment of elements without deviations
options.D: Have the multidisciplinary team monitor the elements continuously at routine meetings throughout the year

questions.explanation: The document suggests that the multidisciplinary team that will take part in the periodic review formally monitor the elements at routine meetings throughout the year, which both accomplishes the effectiveness assessment and reduces the administrative burden.

questions.question: What is one purpose of periodically reviewing the CCS?

options.A: Only to confirm that document version numbers and approval records are complete and filed
options.B: To allow EM sampling quantities and microbiological test items to be reduced after the review to save cost
options.C: To ensure the CCS keeps pace with the process, conforms to industry standards, and assess whether new, more effective technologies should be adopted
options.D: To replace the functions and roles of the quality systems (investigations, change control, CAPA)

questions.explanation: The periodic review ensures the CCS stays in step with the process and consistent with industry standards, in particular assessing whether new, more effective technologies should be adopted. It does not replace the quality systems such as investigations, change control, and CAPA, but evaluates their outputs as a whole.

questions.question: What is the subject of USP general chapter <1231>, listed in TR90 section 14.2.2 (United States)?

options.A: Containers: Glass
options.B: Package integrity evaluation
options.C: Determination of water activity
options.D: Water for pharmaceutical purposes

questions.explanation: TR90 section 5.6 cites USP <1231> Water for Pharmaceutical Purposes as a reference for contamination control of water systems, and it is also listed in section 14.2.2. In the same list, <660> is Containers-Glass, <1207> is Package Integrity Evaluation-Sterile Products, and <1112> is the application of water activity determination to non-sterile pharmaceutical products.

questions.question: What subject does 21 CFR 211.94, cited in the TR90 references, regulate?

options.A: Drug product containers and closures
options.B: cGMP guidance for sterile drug products produced by aseptic processing
options.C: Requirements for equipment cleaning and maintenance
options.D: General principles and practices of process validation

questions.explanation: Reference 20 is 21 CFR 211.94, Drug product containers and closures, which TR90 cites in the container closure section to state that a CC system must not be reactive, additive, or absorptive so as to alter the safety, identity, strength, quality, or purity of the drug, and must provide adequate protection.

questions.question: What test is USP general chapter <63>, cited as TR90 reference 17?

options.A: Sterility test
options.B: Mycoplasma tests
options.C: Microbial enumeration
options.D: Endotoxin test

questions.explanation: Reference 17 is General Chapter <63> Mycoplasma Tests, cited to explain that mycoplasma testing may use culture methods and indicator cell culture methods, and that rapid alternative methods may be used when appropriately validated. The bacterial endotoxins test is a different chapter, USP <85> (reference 6).

questions.question: What is the subject of ISO 14644-1:2015, listed in TR90 section 14.2.1?

options.A: Contaminants and purity classes in compressed air
options.B: Lot-by-lot inspection by attributes sampling procedures indexed by acceptance quality limit (AQL)
options.C: Classification of air cleanliness by particle concentration
options.D: Fundamentals and vocabulary of quality management systems

questions.explanation: ISO 14644-1:2015 is Cleanrooms and Associated Controlled Environments, Part 1: Classification of Air Cleanliness by Particle Concentration. In the same list, ISO 8573-1 covers compressed air, ISO 2859-1 covers attribute sampling, and ISO 9000 covers the fundamentals and vocabulary of quality management systems.

questions.question: What is the subject of ICH Q10, listed in TR90 section 14.2.1?

options.A: Quality risk management
options.B: Pharmaceutical quality system
options.C: Pharmaceutical development
options.D: GMP for active pharmaceutical ingredients

questions.explanation: ICH Q10 is Pharmaceutical Quality System; in the same list Q9 is QRM, Q8(R2) is pharmaceutical development, and Q7 is GMP for active pharmaceutical ingredients. TR90 also notes that the foundational elements of the CCS echo the enablers described in Q10.

questions.topic: Barrier vs UF/BSC for open processes
questions.question: According to Appendix 1 Table 15.0-1, for an open process that directly affects the purity of materials, which approach is preferred?

options.A: Using unidirectional flow devices or biological safety cabinets in preference to barrier technology
options.B: Using barrier technology in preference to unidirectional flow devices or biological safety cabinets
options.C: The three are equally effective, and the choice may be made freely based on cost and availability
options.D: Gowning and aseptic technique alone, with no additional equipment barrier

questions.explanation: The table states that for open processes that directly affect the purity of materials or introduce adventitious agents, barrier technology is preferred over unidirectional flow devices or biological safety cabinets; the latter suit low or controlled bioburden processes, to provide Grade A quality air for critical process steps.

questions.question: According to Table 15.0-4, which kind of packaging material should be prohibited from entering classified areas?

options.A: Material packaged in multiple layers of sterile bags with layers removed one at a time
options.B: Plastic containers and their packaging that can be disinfected
options.C: Packaging that cannot be disinfected and sheds particles, such as cardboard, wood, and open-cell foam
options.D: Double-wrapped material disinfected by wiping with a sporicidal agent

questions.explanation: Table 15.0-4 states that packaging materials that cannot be disinfected and that would carry particles and microorganisms into the facility (such as cardboard, wood, and open-cell foam) should be prohibited. Removing multiple layers of sterile packaging one layer at a time when crossing classification boundaries is the recommended practice.

questions.question: According to Table 15.0-9, what does a "zero CFU" result in environmental monitoring mean?

options.A: It does not guarantee that no microorganisms are present in the environment, because distribution is uneven and detection is limited by sample volume
options.B: It proves that the area is sterile and can be used as the basis for removing the sampling site and subsequent monitoring
options.C: It means viable monitoring has provided real-time results, with no need to wait for incubation and interpretation of results
options.D: It means particle monitoring has identified all genera and species in the environment, with no need for further identification

questions.explanation: The table's "what EM is not" section points out that viable monitoring usually does not give real-time results, particle monitoring is a discrete measurement and cannot provide genus or species, and zero CFU does not guarantee the absence of microorganisms in the environment, because microbial distribution is uneven and detection is limited by sample volume.

questions.question: According to the reminders in Table 15.0-10, which statement about the role of laboratory testing in contamination control is correct?

options.A: Laboratory testing is the main means of contamination control and can replace process and engineering controls
options.B: As long as laboratory tests pass, in-process bioburden control measures and monitoring can be reduced
options.C: The laboratory should intercept contamination in real time during the process to prevent it from entering downstream process steps
options.D: Contamination should not be detected by relying on the laboratory; it should be controlled by process and engineering controls, with testing only verifying their performance

questions.explanation: The table reminds that one should not rely on the laboratory to detect contamination as a process control; process and engineering controls should be established to control bioburden, and laboratory testing only verifies that those controls remain effective.

questions.question: According to Table 15.0-5, how should "return to service" after maintenance work be handled?

options.A: Establish a return-to-service procedure including cleaning, disinfection, and EM, with a walkthrough inspection before release
options.B: A visual check that there is no obvious soiling is enough before production and use resume directly
options.C: Simply remove the maintenance tools, with no cleaning or monitoring, to avoid disturbing the validated state
options.D: Return to service applies only to construction, and general maintenance needs no special procedure or records

questions.explanation: The table requires procedures covering maintenance isolation and return to service, usually including cleaning, disinfection, and EM, with intensity commensurate with risk; spills during maintenance must be dealt with immediately using appropriate cleaning agents and qualified disinfectants, and a walkthrough inspection should be done before release.

questions.topic: When impact assessment does not apply
questions.question: According to Appendix 2, in which situation does microbial impact assessment not apply?

options.A: Bioburden of a non-sterile process intermediate exceeds the established limit
options.B: Bioburden of a chromatography eluate after hold and before filtration exceeds the action limit
options.C: A process step in which no bioburden is expected, such as a cell culture step
options.D: Bioburden of a UF/DF equipment rinse exceeds the process limit for that step

questions.explanation: The document states that for process steps where no bioburden is expected (such as cell culture), a product quality impact assessment does not apply even if no sterility test is performed. For non-sterile process intermediates where microbial control matters, exceeding a bioburden limit often does require an impact assessment.

questions.question: In Example 1, 120 CFU/10 mL of Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was found in an eluate at the end of hold (action value >100 CFU/10 mL). Why was the assessment conclusion "acceptable"?

options.A: Because S. maltophilia produces no by-products such as endotoxin, exotoxin, or protease
options.B: Because the count found was below the action limit, so no further assessment or record is needed
options.C: Because the sterility test of the batch's final product later passed, which is enough to show product quality conforms
options.D: Because the organism did not grow to late exponential phase under eluate conditions, so by-product secretion is unlikely, and downstream filtration removes the cells

questions.explanation: The assessment judged three risk factors: the likelihood of growth to late exponential phase is low (the eluate matrix and 2-8 °C inhibit growth, with endotoxin <0.05 EU/mL); by-product potential is present (can produce endotoxin, exotoxin, and protease); and downstream steps can remove the cells, with accelerated stability showing no protease damage, so severity is low and overall the result is acceptable.

questions.question: According to Appendix 2, what is the approximate minimum concentration at which pathogenic Staphylococcus aureus strains secrete exotoxins?

options.D: 10^10 CFU/mL or more

questions.explanation: Microbial by-products are secreted in a cell-density-dependent manner in late exponential or stationary phase; the document gives as examples that pathogenic S. aureus secretes exotoxin at at least 10^5-10^6 CFU/mL, and Bacillus cereus at at least 10^5 CFU/g. Example 1 uses 10^5 CFU/mL as the worst-case minimum density.

questions.question: When assessing the process removal capability for microbial by-products, the by-product's isoelectric point should be compared with which downstream step?

options.A: A validated chromatography step
options.B: An in-process heating step
options.C: A size-exclusion step
options.D: A 0.2 µm sterilizing filtration step

questions.explanation: The document lists three pairings: the by-product's molecular size corresponds to a size-exclusion step, its heat resistance to a heating step, and its isoelectric point to a validated chromatography step.

questions.question: In Example 2, 20 CFU/100 mL of Sphingomonas paucimobilus was found in an equipment rinse before UF/DF (step limit 10 CFU/100 mL). Why was the overall risk judged low?

options.A: Because the organism is a spore former and is naturally killed under UF/DF conditions
options.B: Because the count found was only slightly above the limit, so only a notification to QA is needed
options.C: Because no batch testing after UF/DF needs to be performed any more
options.D: Because the hold time was short and the organism does not readily proliferate, downstream purification can remove it, and all subsequent tests passed

questions.explanation: Example 2 assesses severity, probability, and downstream control item by item across three risk aspects: count, endotoxin, and other metabolites. The overall risk was low because the hold time was short (<24 hours), the organism would not grow to high numbers, downstream purification steps exist, and all subsequent product tests passed.

questions.question: In the Appendix 3 BFS case, what was the root cause of the sterility failure and the media fill failure?

options.A: High microbial counts in the mold plate cooling water, and pinhole leaks in the mold plate contaminating the product
options.B: Operators not gowning as required in the Grade A area, so that skin flora contaminated the product
options.C: Excess endotoxin in the raw material, released during the BFS process and contaminating the product
options.D: Construction work causing migration of spore formers, contaminating the adjacent BFS aseptic filling area

questions.explanation: The mold plates in the BFS case were cooled with water that had a very high microbial count, and pinhole leaks in the mold plate let the cooling water contaminate the product directly; the main deficiencies were unsuitable equipment and inadequate preventive maintenance. The company found that routine visual inspection for mold leaks was not enough and changed to periodic pressure integrity testing of the mold equipment. The construction scenario belongs to Case Study 3.

questions.question: In the Appendix 3 construction case, what was the company's main GMP failure?

options.A: Continuing to use a gowning room that did not qualify during construction, so that many personnel did not gown as required
options.B: Not adequately assessing the risk of construction to sterility assurance, wrongly assuming it would not affect the product
options.C: Not performing sterility tests on every finished batch, so contamination could not be detected during construction
options.D: Not cleaning the gowning room walls after construction, so residual dust entered endotoxin testing

questions.explanation: The company carried out one month of construction in an area adjacent to the gowning airlock while continuing production, and media fills failed repeatedly (Bacillus sp. isolated); its investigation concluded the contaminants migrated from the construction area. TR90 reminds that any departure from normal conditions should be carefully evaluated by production and quality and formally assessed through the deviation or change control system.

questions.question: Under the classification in Case Study 4, which of the following is an "invasive disruption"?

options.A: Caulk repair
options.B: Light switch repair (without cutting)
options.C: Equipment calibration
options.D: Opening an electrical panel while processing is in progress

questions.explanation: Invasive disruptions are activities that breach the integrity of a controlled classified area or critical utility and are performed while processing is still going on in the room, such as opening an electrical panel; noninvasive disruptions do not breach integrity and are done with no activity in the room, such as caulking, switch or outlet repair (without cutting), and calibration.

questions.question: How should the CCS be adjusted for Process 3 of Appendix 4 (no open steps, pre-assembled single-use assemblies, few manual connections)?

options.A: No additional controls are needed because it is a closed process, and neither consumables nor suppliers need checking
options.B: Cleanroom grade must be raised, and personnel gowning and awareness campaigns strengthened
options.C: Strengthen incoming consumable inspection (such as pre-use inflation checks) and work with the supplier, with a more relaxed classification possible
options.D: Maintenance and equipment audits must both be strengthened, because reusable equipment with complex piping is used

questions.explanation: Appendix 4 explains that the CCS should be tailored to process risk. Process 3 has no open steps, so environmental and personnel risk is lower and a more relaxed cleanroom classification can be used; the main risk is supplier quality defects (such as leaks), so incoming consumable inspection, on-site inflation checks before use, and collaboration with the supplier should be strengthened. Raising the cleanroom grade and strengthening gowning corresponds to Process 1, as do strengthened maintenance and equipment audits, which are the equipment side of Process 1.

questions.question: According to the Appendix 5 template notes, how should CCS documents be written for a multi-product facility whose products differ greatly in process and associated CCS (for example, liquid and solid, non-sterile and sterile products)?

options.A: One document for the whole site, covering all products and processes
options.B: Separate CCS documents prepared for each product
options.C: Written only for the single highest-risk product, with the other products using it by reference
options.D: Written separately by shift or season, with identical content each time

questions.explanation: The template notes state that for a multi-product facility whose processes are similar and use the same CCS (such as fill-finish), one document can cover all products; if processes and associated CCS differ greatly (such as some API sites, liquid and solid products together, or non-sterile and sterile together), a strategy document should be prepared for each product.
